opus-5.5.text:
So the core idea is that you can't compare models fairly unless you hold everything else constant. When people talk about the energy use of AI, they often mix together very different things: different hardware, different batch sizes, different data centers, different tasks. You end up comparing apples and oranges.

What we try to do is standardize the setup. We pick a set of common tasks, like text generation, summarization, image classification, image generation, and so on, and for each task we put together a representative dataset. Then we run every model on the same hardware, with the same configuration, the same number of queries, and we measure the energy actually consumed during inference. We focus on inference because that's where the bulk of the energy goes once a model is deployed. Training is a one-time cost, but inference happens millions or billions of times a day.

For the measurement itself, we use tools that track GPU energy directly, and we also account for CPU and memory where we can, so it's not just a back-of-the-envelope estimate based on hardware specs. Specs tell you peak power draw, but real-world usage can be quite different.

Once we have those numbers, we compare models within the same task, because it doesn't make sense to compare an image generation model to a text classifier. They're doing fundamentally different amounts of work. Within each task, we rank models relative to one another and assign a rating, kind of like the Energy Star labels you see on appliances. That way someone choosing a model, say a developer or a procurement person at a company, can see at a glance whether the model they're considering is on the efficient end or the energy-hungry end for that kind of task.

One of the biggest challenges is closed models. If a model is only available through an API, we can't run it on our own hardware, so we can't measure it the same way. Our approach has been to make the methodology open and to invite companies to run the benchmark themselves and submit results, ideally in a verifiable way. Some have been receptive, others less so. But the goal is really to create a shared, transparent standard, so that energy becomes one of the criteria people look at alongside accuracy and cost when they pick a model.

r001.rationale: It says models are run on the same hardware and GPU energy is tracked, but it does not specify a GPU model.

r002.rationale: It does not mention CodeCarbon or state that emissions estimates depend on how the electricity is generated.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about it is that energy is actually the most concrete thing we can measure, right? When you talk about carbon footprint, you're already adding layers of uncertainty, because carbon depends on where the data center is, what the grid mix looks like at that moment, whether they're buying renewable energy certificates, and so on. But energy, kilowatt-hours, that's something you can actually measure at the hardware level.

So what we do, and what I've been proposing for the ratings, is that you take a model, you deploy it on a given piece of hardware, and you run a standardized set of tasks through it. You measure the energy consumed by the GPU, ideally also by the CPU and the RAM, over that workload. And then you report it per query, or per thousand queries, or per token, whatever unit makes sense for the task. We used a tool called CodeCarbon for a lot of this work, and it essentially hooks into the hardware counters to track power draw in real time.

And then the idea with a rating system, and I keep coming back to the Energy Star analogy, is that you don't want people to have to interpret a bunch of numbers. Nobody looks at their fridge and goes, "oh, three hundred and fifty kilowatt-hours a year, is that good?" You want to be able to say: for this type of task, say text generation or image generation, this model is in the top tier for efficiency, and this one is in the bottom tier. So we define the task categories, we have a shared test set, and we compare models within a category, not across categories, because obviously generating an image is going to cost a lot more than classifying a sentence.

The tricky part, honestly, is the hardware dependence. The same model will use a different amount of energy on an A100 versus an H100 versus whatever comes next. So we try to be very explicit about fixing the hardware for the comparison, and then over time you can re-run the evaluation as new hardware comes out. And the other tricky part is closed models, because if you can't run the model yourself, you can't measure it. So a big part of this is also advocating for companies to either report these numbers or allow third parties to measure them, because right now we're mostly in the dark about the models that people use the most.

r001.rationale: The response says to run the model on fixed hardware, measure GPU energy, and gives specific GPU examples such as the A100 and H100.

r002.rationale: It says carbon footprint depends on the data center location and grid mix, but does not connect those factors to CodeCarbon’s estimate of carbon emissions.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by distinguishing training from inference. Training is a large, upfront energy cost, whereas inference is the energy used each time someone interacts with a model. For a rating that helps people choose which model to use, we need to measure inference under comparable conditions.

The idea is to run models on a common set of tasks, measure the energy consumed, and normalize that by the amount of work they do—for example, a fixed number of requests. You also have to control for things like hardware, batch size, and input and output length, because those can substantially change the result.

Then you can compare models within a task, alongside their performance. The point is to help someone ask, ‘What’s the most energy-efficient model that meets my needs?’ And I’d keep energy use distinct from carbon emissions: emissions also depend on where and when that electricity is generated.

r001.rationale: The response says to control for hardware but does not specify a GPU model for the measurement.

r002.rationale: It says emissions depend on where and when electricity is generated, but does not mention CodeCarbon or its estimate.

sol-6.1.text:
The idea is to measure the energy a model uses when you actually run it on a task. We run models on the same hardware, with the same set of inputs, so we can make a meaningful comparison. And we do that across tasks, because generating an image and classifying a piece of text have very different energy requirements.

Then we want to translate those measurements into a rating that’s easy to understand, like an energy-efficiency label on an appliance. So you can consider energy use alongside accuracy and choose a model that does what you need without using more energy than necessary.

r001.rationale: The response says models are run on the same hardware, but does not specify a GPU model.

r002.rationale: It does not mention CodeCarbon, carbon emissions, or how electricity generation affects emissions estimates.
